query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-accuracy machine-learning interatomic potential trained on high-temperature DFT data can reproduce melting properties (melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change at melting) of high-melting refractory alloys with near first‐principles accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of full ab initio free-energy methods.
generation.material_initial_state: High-melting refractory alloy in its solid phase (at temperatures well below the melting point).
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., a moment tensor potential or neural network potential) trained on a curated set of high-temperature DFT data, then use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations combined with thermodynamic integration to compute the melting properties.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted in ensembles (e.g., NPT or NVT) over a temperature range that spans the expected melting point, ensuring sufficient sampling of solid and liquid phases.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic configurations and interatomic force landscapes as represented by the machine-learning potential.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential, trained on high-fidelity DFT data, can accurately reproduce the free energy differences between the solid and liquid states. This allows for efficient thermodynamic integration to extract the melting temperature, as well as derived properties like fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change at melting, while drastically reducing computational expense.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML-based method will yield melting property predictions (melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change) that are within an acceptable error margin compared to the more computationally expensive DFT free-energy calculations, enabling high-throughput screening of refractory alloys.
generation.baseline: Traditional ab initio free-energy methods based on DFT with full thermodynamic integration.
generation.boundary: The approach may be limited if the DFT training set does not span the complete diversity of high-temperature atomic environments in refractory alloys or when extrapolating to compositions substantially outside the training domain.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative error margins of the ML-derived properties relative to full DFT integrations remain uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Train a machine-learning interatomic potential using a comprehensive set of high-temperature DFT data for a representative refractory alloy. Perform large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with the ML potential to compute the melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change at melting via thermodynamic integration. Parallelly, perform a set of ab initio free-energy calculations using full DFT thermodynamic integration (or use available experimental data) for the same alloy. Compare the two sets of results.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the melting properties predicted by the ML-based method deviate by more than an acceptable pre-defined error margin (e.g., >10% deviation) from the results of full DFT free-energy calculations or experimental values, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Early efforts to identify high-melting refractory alloys relied on ab initio calculations (DFT-based free energies) and high-throughput screening of potential compositions (as in PMC8282813), but these methods were computationally demanding for large design spaces. Subsequent work (PMC8357793) introduced machine-learning-derived interatomic potentials to capture complex, high-temperature processes in MoNbTaW with near first-principles accuracy at reduced cost. More recent simulations (PMC11375216) further combined classical MD/MC approaches to investigate high-temperature thermal properties (e.g., thermal conductivity) for HfNbTaTiZr, illustrating continued progress in bridging quantum-level accuracy and scalable computational efficiency. Despite these advances, fully accurate and high-throughput determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volumetric changes near melting remains a challenge.
decision.unsolved: A key difficulty is to obtain free energies with near DFT-level accuracy across large composition spaces and temperatures without incurring prohibitive computational costs. Methods to combine advanced sampling with validated machine-learning potentials require more robust training sets, verification, and standardization across the relevant temperature and composition regimes for refractory alloys.
decision.lever: Train and deploy a high-accuracy machine-learning interatomic potential (e.g., moment tensor potential or neural network potential) on DFT data, then use it for large-scale molecular dynamics to compute melting temperature, entropy, enthalpy, and volume change at the melting point. Key parameters include carefully curated high-temperature DFT data, a comprehensive range of atomic environments for training, and robust validation of melting predictions.
decision.why: Machine-learning potentials provide near first-principles fidelity at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling thermodynamic integration and high-throughput simulations of melting in complex, high-melting refractory alloys where full ab initio free-energy methods are impractical.
